set.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels, sometimes 4: one from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three down the gully just east of the top of the Northeast Couloir to the snow. Anchors are natural and may need rigging. Some parties instead make two rappels down slabs north of the east gully and traverse a wet ledge into it.
set.rappel_count_note: The stations follow the usual descent: one rappel to the southeast-face ledge, then down the gully east of the couloir’s top, where two or three single-rope rappels reach the snow, so 3-4 rappels in all. Anchors are natural and not guaranteed to be in place; carry webbing and nuts. The other line, two rappels down slabs north of the east gully off slung blocks and a small tree, then a protected wet-ledge traverse into the gully, is an alternative, not a continuation.
set.descent: One rappel from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three single-rope rappels down the gully east of the couloir’s top to the snow, and a long glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Lake and out the Colchuck Lake trail.
set.descent_text: From the summit, descend back to the upper rock band and make a single rappel to the ledge on the southeast face; you may need to rig a natural anchor, and one party used a slung tree there. Then head over to the top of the Northeast Couloir and find the gully just east of it: two or three single-rope rappels down that gully reach the snow slopes below. Anchors are natural and not reliably in place, so carry webbing and nuts to build them. Alternatively, some parties make two rappels down the slabs just north of the east gully, off slings around blocks and a small tree, then traverse a wet, snow-covered ledge into the gully. Either way, finish with a roughly 2,500 ft glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to the lake, then out via the Colchuck Lake trail. Another option drops via a different gully into Porcupine Creek Basin with a traverse around Colchuck Peak.
